books.section: Topic 4.3 Politics and Regional Interests, A. The Persistence of Regional Priorities
Topic 4.2 The Rise of Political Parties and the Era of Jefferson, The Decline of the Federalist Party and the Era of Good Feelings
A Federalist Debacle and the Era of Good Feelings

stimulus.text: Paraphrase of the report of the Hartford Convention, January 1815: Delegates from New England states, meeting while the War of 1812 was still being fought, complained that embargoes and the war had ruined their trade. They proposed amending the Constitution so that Congress would need a two-thirds vote to declare war, admit new states, or restrict trade with other nations.
stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of the Report of the Hartford Convention (January 1815). Public domain; paraphrased, not quoted.

source: original; stimulus paraphrases the Report of the Hartford Convention, January 1815 (public domain); question 0842 reworked from staged item pr25e-ch08-q03
stem: The Hartford Convention best illustrates the larger pattern that

options.text: New Englanders always supported the federal government in wartime without exception
options.misconception: The convention is New Englanders opposing a war; always supported is the reverse of the evidence.

options.text: regional interests could outweigh loyalty to national policy, even in wartime
the Federalists controlled national politics after 1815
options.misconception: The Federalists collapsed after 1815; Monroe won the presidency almost unopposed.

options.text: the war with Britain united every region behind Madison
options.misconception: New England opposed the war openly; the convention proves the country was not united.

rationales.A: The convention exists because New Englanders did not support this war. A pattern of always supporting wartime policy cannot include the men who protested it.
rationales.B: New England merchants put their trade ahead of Madison’s war, meeting to demand constitutional limits on war and embargoes. The same pattern returns in the tariff fights and the Missouri crisis: region first, nation second.
rationales.C: After 1815 the Federalists held almost nothing. Monroe won in 1816 and again in 1820, and the party soon vanished.
rationales.D: The war divided the country by region. The South and West wanted it; New England opposed it and met at Hartford to say so.
rationales.general:
1. Ask what the delegates chose. They met to limit a war their trade could not afford.
2. Ask what they set aside. Loyalty to the national war policy, in wartime itself.
3. Ask whether the pattern repeats. The South later put cotton ahead of the tariff.
4. Put it together. Hartford is the early case of a pattern running through the period.
Background: the War of 1812 split the country by region, with New England merchants opposing a war the South and West wanted.
Remember: one case is an anecdote, so ask whether the pattern shows up again.
